_about: Extra 'learn more' text for each card's page at tokenstcg.com/learn/<card>/. Keys are card file names (as in design/icons/README.md). Rebuild with: node tools/build-learn.js

not-alive.example: A chatbot can write "I'm so happy to help!" but it doesn't feel happy. It picked words that usually come next in friendly messages.
not-alive.try: List three things you did today that need being alive: feeling hungry, being tired, missing someone. Could an AI really do any of them?

the-human-trainer.example: Before a photo app can find "dogs" in your pictures, people somewhere labeled thousands of photos as dog or not-dog.
the-human-trainer.try: Sort the snacks in your lunch into "healthy" and "treat." Did a classmate sort them the same way? An AI learns whatever labels its trainers choose.

human-in-the-loop.example: A bank's AI may flag a purchase as fraud, but a person checks before your card is actually blocked.
human-in-the-loop.try: Name one decision you'd let an AI make alone and one you'd always want a person to check. What makes them different?

chatbot.example: The help bubble on a store's website that answers "Where's my order?" is often a chatbot.
chatbot.try: Write one question a chatbot would answer well and one it would probably get wrong. Why the difference?

agent.example: A robot vacuum senses walls, decides where to go next, and moves on its own. That's an agent.
agent.try: Pick a robot or app you know. What does it sense? What does it decide? What action does it take?

ai-career-path.example: AI teams include people who label data, test for problems, design how the app looks, write rules for safety, and explain AI to the public.
ai-career-path.try: Pick something you're already good at, like drawing, arguing, organizing, or helping friends. How could that skill help build better AI?

manual-override.example: Self-driving test cars have a safety driver who can grab the wheel and take over at any moment.
manual-override.try: Think of a machine with an off switch or an "undo" button. Why did its designers add one?

ai-isn-t-magic.example: When a chatbot answers a question, it isn't thinking it over. It's predicting likely words, very quickly, using patterns from text it read.
ai-isn-t-magic.try: Write down something people say AI can do. Then ask: who built it, and what did it learn from?

python.example: Many AI projects, from school robotics clubs to big research labs, are written in the Python programming language.
python.try: Write the steps for making a sandwich so exactly that a robot could follow them. That's what programming feels like.

fast-moving-lab.example: Some AI companies release new tools every few months, racing to be first.
fast-moving-lab.try: List one good thing and one risky thing about releasing a new AI tool to everyone very quickly.

safety-lab.example: Some AI teams spend time testing for harmful answers and fixing them before a tool is released.
safety-lab.try: If you were testing a new AI homework helper before release, what are three things you'd check first?

ai-assistant.example: AI assistants can draft an email, explain a hard paragraph, or brainstorm ideas for a project.
ai-assistant.try: Name one way an assistant could help you learn, and one way it could stop you from learning. Where's the line?

viral-app.example: Some AI chatbot apps gained millions of users within weeks of launching, faster than almost any app before them.
viral-app.try: Why do some apps spread so fast? List three reasons, then decide whether fast is good, bad, or both.

built-in-ai.example: Autocomplete in a search bar and suggested replies in email are AI built into tools you already use.
built-in-ai.try: Look at one app on a phone or computer. Find one feature that's probably AI. How can you tell?

defunct.example: When an app shuts down, the photos, messages, or progress you kept there can disappear with it.
defunct.try: Think of an app or game you used that's gone or changed a lot. What happened to your stuff?

abstraction.example: A subway map leaves out streets and buildings so you can focus on the stops. AI models simplify the world in the same way.
abstraction.try: Draw a map from your home to school using only five things. What did you leave out, and why?

feature-vector.example: To a computer, a song might be a list of numbers: how fast it is, how loud it is, how much singing it has.
feature-vector.try: Describe your favorite animal using only three numbers from 1 to 10, like size, speed, and fluffiness. Can a friend guess it?

classifier.example: Email spam filters sort each message into "spam" or "not spam."
classifier.try: Make two piles of objects on your desk using one rule. Have a friend guess the rule. That's what a classifier learns.

predictor.example: A maps app predicts how many minutes your trip will take. That's a number, not a category.
predictor.try: Predict how many minutes the walk home will take today. What clues did you use? A predictor uses clues the same way.

recommender.example: "Because you watched…" rows on video apps come from a recommender.
recommender.try: Recommend a book or show to a friend. How did you decide? Was it what they liked before, or what people like them liked?

decision-tree.example: "Is it raining? Yes → take an umbrella. No → is it cold? Yes → take a jacket" is a tiny decision tree.
decision-tree.try: Make a three-question yes/no tree that decides what to eat for lunch. Can a friend follow it and get the same answer?

search-tree.example: Game-playing AIs look ahead at possible moves, like "if I go here, they'll go there," to pick the best one.
search-tree.try: Play tic-tac-toe and say your thinking out loud: "If I go here, they could…" You're searching a tree.

ambiguous-input.example: A voice assistant might mishear "write" as "right" when there's background noise.
ambiguous-input.try: Say a sentence with a word that has two meanings, like "bat" or "bark." How did your listener know which one you meant?

discontinued.example: When a company stops supporting a gadget, it may stop getting updates and safety fixes, even though it still turns on.
discontinued.try: Why might a company warn people before it stops supporting something? Write the warning message you'd send.

sensor.example: Phones have cameras, microphones, touch screens, and motion sensors that all turn the real world into data.
sensor.try: Name every sensor you can think of in a phone or a car. What does each one sense?

training-data.example: A photo app learns what cats look like from thousands of example cat photos.
training-data.try: If you had to teach an AI what a "good drawing" is, what ten examples would you show it? Would everyone pick the same ten?

bias-in-data.example: If face photos used for training are mostly of one group of people, a face-recognition system may work worse for others.
bias-in-data.try: Imagine an AI that learned what a "teacher" looks like only from your school. Who might it wrongly decide isn't a teacher?

supervised-learning.example: Showing an AI thousands of emails already labeled "spam" or "not spam" until it learns the difference.
supervised-learning.try: Teach a friend a made-up rule using examples only: show items labeled "blip" or "not blip" until they can guess.

neural-network.example: Image and speech recognition in many apps run on neural networks with millions of tiny connected parts.
neural-network.try: Line up five classmates. Each one passes a message along, changing it a little. A neural network passes numbers through layers like that.

large-language-model.example: Chatbots that can write stories or explain homework are usually built on large language models.
large-language-model.try: Start a sentence and let classmates add one word at a time. You're predicting the next word, the way an LLM does.

reinforcement-learning.example: An AI can learn to play a video game by trying moves over and over and getting points when it does well.
reinforcement-learning.try: Teach a friend to find a hidden object using only "warmer" and "colder." That's learning from rewards.

retraining-pause.example: Apps sometimes switch off an AI feature for a while to fix problems and update it.
retraining-pause.try: Why might a company pause an AI tool instead of fixing it while people keep using it?

neuron.example: One artificial neuron just adds up some numbers and decides how strongly to pass a signal on. The power comes from millions working together.
neuron.try: Be a neuron: a friend holds up fingers on each hand. Add them up, and if the total is more than 5, clap. That's one neuron's job.

tensor.example: A color photo is stored as a grid of numbers for every pixel, three layers deep for red, green, and blue. That's a tensor.
tensor.try: Draw a 4×4 grid and fill it with 0s and 1s to make a smiley face. You just stored an image as numbers.

cuda.example: Tools that let AI run on graphics chips are a big reason training that once took weeks can take days.
cuda.try: Time how long it takes one person to sort a deck of cards, then four people splitting it. Why is splitting the work faster?

imagenet.example: A huge collection of labeled photos, used in a famous image-recognition contest, helped spark today's AI boom.
imagenet.try: If you built a photo collection to teach AI about food, what foods might you forget to include? Who would that leave out?

gan.example: Some realistic fake faces online were made by two AIs competing: one makes fakes, the other tries to catch them.
gan.try: Play "forger and detective": one person draws a fake signature, another tries to spot it. Both get better each round.

diffusion-model.example: Many AI image tools start with random static and clean it up, step by step, into a picture.
diffusion-model.try: Start with a page of random scribbles and slowly turn them into a drawing. That's roughly how a diffusion model works.

unsupervised-learning.example: A store's AI might notice groups of shoppers who buy similar things, without anyone telling it what the groups are.
unsupervised-learning.try: Dump a pile of mixed objects and sort them into groups without being given any rules. What groups did you invent?

transformer.example: Transformers help chatbots figure out which earlier words matter. In "The dog chased the ball until it was tired," what is "it"?
transformer.try: Read a sentence and underline the words that matter most for its meaning. That's what attention does.

gpt.example: GPT stands for Generative Pre-trained Transformer: an AI that read a huge amount of text first, then learned to generate new text.
gpt.try: Explain "pre-trained" to a friend using sports practice as an example. Why practice before the real game?

gpu.example: Chips first built for video-game graphics turned out to be great at the math AI needs, because they do thousands of small calculations at once.
gpu.try: Have one person add up ten numbers while ten people each add one pair at the same time. Which finishes first?

cpu.example: The CPU runs your computer's programs step by step: opening apps, saving files, following instructions in order.
cpu.try: Follow a recipe one step at a time, in order. That's how a CPU works. What steps could two people do at the same time?

ram.example: RAM holds whatever the computer is working on right now, and it's wiped when the power goes off.
ram.try: Remember a 7-digit number for 30 seconds without writing it down. Your short-term memory is like RAM.

embedding.example: In an AI's number map of words, "dog" ends up close to "puppy" and far from "airplane."
embedding.try: Place these words on a line from "tiny" to "huge": ant, cat, horse, whale, mouse. You just made a simple embedding.

fine-tuning.example: A general chatbot can be trained a bit more on medical questions to become a better health-info helper.
fine-tuning.try: You already know how to read. What extra practice would make you an expert at reading maps? That's fine-tuning.

outdated.example: An AI trained a few years ago might not know about new games, events, or the latest phones.
outdated.try: Write three things that changed in the last year. Would an AI trained before then know about them?

fairness-check.example: Before using an AI to help choose who gets a loan, testers check whether it treats different groups of people equally.
fairness-check.try: Is it fair if everyone gets the same thing, or if everyone gets what they need? Argue both sides for one minute each.

bias-audit.example: Reviewers test a hiring AI with matching résumés that differ only in the name, to see if it treats them differently.
bias-audit.try: Design a quick test to check whether a school-photo AI recognizes everyone in your class equally well.

model-card.example: A model card is like a nutrition label for AI. It tells what the model is for, what data it learned from, and where it doesn't work well.
model-card.try: Write a mini "model card" for yourself as a helper: what you're good at, what you're not, and what you shouldn't be asked to do.

explainability.example: If an AI says a photo shows a wolf, an explainable system can show it looked at the snow in the background, which is a clue that it may be wrong.
explainability.try: Make a decision, like what to eat, and explain it in three reasons. Would a friend trust your choice more after hearing them?

privacy-shield.example: Some AI systems remove names and blur faces before using data, so people can't be identified.
privacy-shield.try: List three pieces of information about you that you'd never want used to train an AI. Why those?

accountability.example: When an automated system makes a harmful mistake, people argue over who's responsible: the company, the designer, or the user.
accountability.try: A self-driving bus misses a stop. Who should fix it, and who should apologize? Are those the same person?

ethical-framework.example: Many organizations publish AI principles, such as fairness, safety, privacy, and transparency, to guide what they build.
ethical-framework.try: Write three rules every AI at your school must follow. Rank them: which matters most?

compliance-review.example: Before some AI tools can be used in schools or hospitals, they're checked against privacy and safety rules.
compliance-review.try: Make a five-item checklist an AI homework app must pass before your school allows it.

mandatory-recall.example: Cars and toys can be recalled when they're found unsafe. Some people think AI products should work the same way.
mandatory-recall.try: What would an AI app have to do before you'd want it recalled? Draw your line.

informed-consent.example: Some apps ask before using your photos or recordings to improve their AI, and some don't ask clearly at all.
informed-consent.try: Rewrite a confusing permission pop-up so a 10-year-old would understand exactly what they're agreeing to.

red-teaming.example: Companies hire testers to try to trick a chatbot into breaking its own rules, so the holes get fixed before release.
red-teaming.try: Think like a tester: how might someone trick a homework chatbot into just giving the answers? How would you block that?

expired.example: Some permissions, like sharing your location, can be set to end after a while instead of lasting forever.
expired.try: Should permission to use your data run out? Pick a time limit for photos, location, and messages, and explain your choices.

ai-in-daily-life.example: Autocorrect, music suggestions, spam filters, and photo search are AI you may use every day without noticing.
ai-in-daily-life.try: Keep a tally for one day: every time you notice AI, write it down. How many did you find?

deepfake.example: AI can make realistic videos or voice clips of people saying things they never said.
deepfake.try: Before sharing a surprising video, what three checks would you do? Write your own "pause before posting" checklist.

job-disruption.example: AI can now do some tasks, like sorting documents or writing simple reports, that used to take people hours.
job-disruption.try: Pick a job you might want. Which parts could AI help with, and which parts need a person?

environmental-footprint.example: Running large AI models uses a lot of electricity, and the computers often need water for cooling.
environmental-footprint.try: List three times you used AI this week. Which ones were worth the energy, and which weren't?

data-privacy-trade-off.example: Many free apps are paid for with data about what you do, which can be used to target ads or train AI.
data-privacy-trade-off.try: Pick a free app you use. What do you think it learns about you? Would you pay a dollar a month to keep that private?

regulation-debate.example: Governments around the world are debating laws about AI, like labeling AI-made images or limiting facial recognition.
regulation-debate.try: Write one AI law you'd pass for kids your age. Who would agree with it, and who might argue against it?

digital-divide.example: Students without fast internet or a computer at home can't use AI learning tools the way others can.
digital-divide.try: What would a school need to do so every student gets the same chance to learn about AI? List three steps.

cognitive-offload.example: If you always let a map app give directions, you may never learn your way around your own town.
cognitive-offload.try: Pick one skill you'd never want AI to do for you, and one you're happy to hand off. What's the difference?

data-center.example: Huge buildings full of computers run the AI apps people use. They need lots of power and cooling.
data-center.try: A company wants to build a data center in your town. List one benefit and one concern.

obsolete.example: Floppy disks once saved everyone's files. Today they mostly survive as the "Save" icon.
obsolete.try: Ask an adult about a gadget they used that's now obsolete. What replaced it, and why?

alignment.example: An AI told to "keep people watching" might show videos that keep kids up too late. It did what it was told, not what people wanted.
alignment.try: Write a goal for a cleaning robot. Then try to find a sneaky way it could follow your words but miss your point.
